https://www.forbes.com/sites/antoniopequ.text: Breaking Business Apache Helicopter Crash In Texas Leaves 2 Dead By Antonio Pequeño IV , Forbes Staff. Pequeño is a breaking news reporter who covers tech and more. Follow Author Aug 12, 2026, 06:32pm EDT Aug 12, 2026, 07:27pm EDT Topline An attack helicopter from the U.S. Army base Fort Hood crashed near the installation Wednesday, according to multiple reports , killing both of its pilots. A US Army AH-64D Apache helicopter hovers flies during military exercises of Poland and NATO allied countries in Orzysz, northwestern Poland, on September 17, 2025. Photo by Wojtek RADWANSKI / AFP) Key Facts The crash triggered a blaze that has burned about 100 acres of land north of Austin, Texas, according to data from the Texas A&M Forest Service Incident Viewer. Cliff Coleman, a spokesperson for the Bell County Sheriff’s Office, told reporters the helicopter landed in a field, calling it a “violent crash.” The helicopter involved in the crash is the AH-64 Apache, which carries a pilot and a co-pilot and is meant for reconnaissance, attacks on armored targets and aerial support for ground troops. The crash took place around 1:35 p.m. local time and the pilots were pronounced dead nearly an hour later, Coleman said. Forbes has reached out to the Army for comment. What We Don’t Know It is unclear where the helicopter was going or what the reason for its deployment was. Coleman deferred several questions about the situation to Army authorities at Fort Hood who are investigating the crash. Key Background Foot Hood spans over 218,000 acres and is used to train active-duty troops and armored vehicle crews. Nearly 40,000 soldiers are stationed at the base, according to the Army’s website, and it is the only Army installation with the capacity to station and train two armored divisions. Apache helicopters like the one that crashed Wednesday have been used in the war against Iran, which has likely increased training activity for pilots and movements of the aircraft within U.S. airspace. A spike in military aircraft accidents occurred in 2024, according to an Associated Press report that cited internal Pentagon figures, with the rate of severe accidents per 100,000 flight hours jumping 55% in the 2024 budget year compared to the four previous years. The Army had the second-most accidents that year, though the Marines’ rate was nearly double that of the Army, Air Force and Navy. https://www.dw.com/en/poland-wants-india.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Oh0P Prefer DW on Google India and Poland have good ties despite conflicting stances on Ukraine Image: Manish Swarup/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement During his recent visit to India , Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk seemingly went out of his way to ingratiate himself to Narendra Modi , describing the Indian leader as a "beacon of hope" in the times of global uncertainty and instability. One of the issues the two prime ministers discussed was the war in Ukraine , a country bordering Poland which Warsaw supports diplomatically and militarily against Russia . "We will support all efforts aimed at achieving peace," Modi said during the joint press briefing. Russia ramps up drone war with new launch megabase To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Previous reports indicated India had formulated a plan to halt strikes on energy infrastructure between Russia and Ukraine and protect ships transporting grain and fuel. Before traveling to New Delhi, Tusk had also indicated that India "could play a constructive role" regarding the war, saying that this aspect was "very important" to him. While no concrete steps were announced during his trip, many in Europe still hope India can use its friendship with Russia to boost peace talks . Analysts warn, however, that New Delhi's access to the Kremlin does not automatically grant it sway over Russian President Vladimir Putin and his decisions. India 'cannot guarantee peace' India is unlikely to sacrifice its own interests at Europe's insistence, says India's former ambassador to Poland Anil Wadhwa. So far, New Delhi has maintained its political and defense relationship with Moscow while calling for dialogue and diplomacy and resisting pressure to align fully with Western sanctions . Moreover, while New Delhi may be able to communicate with both Moscow and Kyiv, there is no guarantee either side will respond to its efforts or make concessions. " Poland wants India to use its access to Vladimir Putin to encourage a ceasefire and meaningful negotiations, while recognizing the limits of New Delhi's influence over Russian military decisions," he told DW. Poland's ex-president: Putin's war in Ukraine was a miscalculation To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The challenge, Wadhwa said, was to translate India's diplomatic access into practical outcomes without expecting too much. "India can contribute to de-escalation and help create conditions for negotiations, but it cannot guarantee peace," he said. Europe moves closer to India despite Russia row The Polish initiative also reflects a wider European effort to deepen relations with India. Ummu Salma Bava, chairperson and Jean Monnet Chair at the Centre for European Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University, told DW that Tusk's visit had two objectives: strengthening ties between India and his own country and persuading New Delhi to factor in the EU's perspective on the Ukraine war. "The Ukraine war has become central to European security. India's strong association with Moscow despite the war has raised concerns on developing cooperation on security between India and the EU," Bava said. Poland, a frontline state, does not want Russia to gain additional economic benefits from its relationship with India. Trump announces 'energy ceasefire' in Ukraine war To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video So far, according to Bava, "both sides have managed to compartmentalize the Ukraine issue" while advancing cooperation on trade, security and defense. But their differences could complicate future efforts to expand defense and security cooperation, she warned. US shift on Ukraine lets EU allies change stance Ajay Bisaria, another former envoy to Poland, says India's position has "matured into that of a potential peacemaker" and its ability to communicate with both Kyiv and Moscow is now perceived as useful. According to Bisaria, not even Warsaw regards "the Russia question" as a "significant irritant in the India-Europe or India-Poland relationship." "Europe, and Poland in particular, understands the depth of India's partnership with Russia, just as India appreciates the very different lens through which much of Europe views Moscow and the war in Ukraine," Bisaria told DW. How Trump is helping Putin To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video This shift in perspective, according to Bisaria, is partly due to the US changing its own stance on the conflict and seeking mediation . This, in his view, strengthens the case for European governments to pursue close ties with India despite their differences over Moscow.
